items.question: What did working on SmartMoney's website teach you about the value of data visualization?
items.object: Data visualization in financial journalism
items.answer: While I was there, one of the things that I discovered—we, because there was a great team—was that if you could visualize, just in terms of charts and graphs, what was going on in the market or for a personal investment decision, that made a huge impact on people who were reading the online magazine. They could understand all sorts of complicated things that were just hard to get across in pure words. So that sparked an interest for me in data visualization, and I started doing fancier and fancier charts and graphs, weirder and weirder things. items.question: How has Irene Greif's perspective on people using computers together influenced your thinking?
items.object: Irene Greif's perspective on collaborative computer use
items.answer: I was in a group that was related to collaboration. It was run by a woman named Irene Greif, who pioneered the idea that when we think about people using computers, it's not just a matter of a single person using a single computer or a single person using a cluster, but many people using computers together, and that the dynamics of multiple people are really complicated and important and interesting to study. That, I think, has infused a lot of my work since then, both in visualization and in machine learning.

items.question: How did you weigh your enthusiasm for neural networks against their career prospects when you studied them in the 1980s?
items.object: Neural networks as a career prospect in the 1980s
items.answer: I had had a brief spate of interest in machine learning in college. Very long ago, I even took a course in neural networks, and this was in the 1980s, so this was really the olden days. I remember at the time just loving the topic so much and yet feeling like, oh, I don't know, maybe the whole thing is just a dead end. Do I really want to bet my career on this? items.object: Skepticism about neural networks in the 1980s
items.answer: Yeah, I'm trying to remember the dynamic exactly. I think this was post-backpropagation. I remember Yann's name coming up, for sure. The other thing that was true is that there was just very little computing power. items.question: How do you think visual hierarchy helps you design effective data visualizations?
items.object: Visual hierarchy in data visualization
items.answer: As I was designing visualizations, the question is always, how can we design them better? How can we do things that are really effective in making people feel smarter? In order to do that, you pretty quickly realize, oh, I need to understand something about what's going on in people's heads. What is their mental model of the world? What is vision doing? What special powers does our visual system have? One of the things that becomes clear when you start doing design is exactly this idea of hierarchy, and this is something that I still try to get across in any design class I teach, or working with students on creating diagrams: when you first look at an image, you see large structure. Then your eye will sort of traverse it in certain ways, and you can pick out a part that you're interested in. You can look at smaller things, and if you have a well-designed diagram, you can organize a huge amount of information that way and basically guide a person's eye to what is most important. This is all sort of designer intuition, which I certainly did not make up. This is known by designers informally for a very long time.

items.question: What did working on your multiscale model of perceptual organization teach you about understanding how people use visualizations?
items.object: The multiscale model of perceptual organization and the limits of mathematical approaches to visualization design
items.answer: One of the things I was trying to do with this paper is formalize that designer intuition and say, okay, can we actually take some relatively sophisticated geometrical techniques that have been developed for computer vision, a notion of scale space, come up with an actual model of what might be in your head or what a designer might think of, and then surface that to someone who is designing a visualization? I think the good news about that paper is that we actually were able to come up with a model that matched our intuitions a little bit, that was able to give the right answer in some simple cases. I felt like that's an interesting direction to go. However, I will also say in the process of writing this paper, it just became clear to me that I was hoping for way too much in our then understanding of the human visual system. There was no way that I was at that point going to write a program that would simulate what goes through someone's head when they see a data visualization. In some ways I feel like one lesson I learned from that is that you can't have too high a hope for just a quantitative answer to everything. At some level in visualization design, you just have to rely on qualitative studies. You have to rely on designer intuition for the moment, at least; there's no way around it. Maybe this will all be changed in a couple of decades or something. But for me, coming from a mathematical background where I felt like, of course you want everything to be quantitative, of course you want everything to be mathematical, this was one of the points where I really learned, okay, you can try that, you can push that pretty far. At the end of the day, if you really want to understand what's going on, qualitative understanding—just talking to someone and watching them use a visualization for five minutes—is probably going to be more informative than plugging the image into a fancy mathematical model.

items.question: How do you decide how much information to put into a visualization without overwhelming its audience?
items.object: Audience-dependent information density in visualization design
items.answer: I think the best way to attack that question is to think about who your audience is, because different audiences really respond in different ways. If your audience is encountering complicated information for the first time, and I'll give you an example: imagine someone who's planning for retirement. This is something that we thought about when I was at SmartMoney. I watched other people design retirement calculators and retirement predictors. That's really overwhelming to a lot of people, and very frequently the truth is that predicting the future is incredibly hard and there are so many variables. It's really tempting to just put all of those variables into one big worksheet that is very off-putting for a lot of people. Frequently, you can get a lot of the value just giving people a sense of, okay, look, you're going to need to save money. Here's what's going to happen. Here's what it means to draw down savings, with relatively few variables. That's very typical: if you're introducing something for the first time, maybe someone is only going to see something once, that's when you want to really aim for simplicity in the sense of relatively sparse, carefully curated information. On the other hand, there's another kind of chart you might use, which is for someone who is monitoring something, who looks at that all the time, becomes an expert in the field. Maybe they look at their stock portfolio every day, or they're a data analyst and it's their job to look at a lot of information, trying to understand what's going on. In this case, you want to put as much information as you can on the screen. Every person I've worked with who is an expert, who is looking at things, I've never heard anyone as an expert say, I want to see less. What you do want to do, though, is organize things so that they can find it relatively easily, so that it makes sense. In a sense, I don't think there's a right answer to how much information should I put on the screen until you start looking at who the person is who is going to be using your visualization.

items.question: How do you decide how much data a visualization should show?
items.object: How much data to include in a visualization
items.answer: I do think that typically people will underestimate how much information people can handle. In general, if I had to give one piece of advice to people who are starting to create their own visualizations, it would be: show more data rather than less data. The biggest mistake is people try to make things too simple. The thing that I would also add there is that there's also a distinction between data analysis and communicating a point. Often when you're communicating a point, you can make things much, much simpler because there's interesting stuff, but it's just not relevant, and you can take it away because you know what you want to communicate. On the other hand, when you're giving people data to analyze, you don't know a priori what's going to be useful. So that's again the case where I'd say give them a lot of information.

items.question: How do you think about data visualization as a rhetorical process?
items.object: Rhetoric and editorial choices in data visualization
items.answer: I think it's ultimately a rhetorical process. Unless you're designing some pure data analysis tool—and then probably even then—but if you are, say, at a newspaper and you are creating a visualization to accompany a story, that's rhetoric. You're making decisions about what to include, what is important, what is not important, and it's always important to keep that in mind. Also as a reader, what do they leave out of the visualization? How did they choose the bounds on that x-axis? Why did they start it that year? That's almost always the tell, by the way, because frequently you can really change what the message is with a time series by choosing the date boundaries. You can often tell what people are trying to get across by looking at it carefully. Sometimes you'll see these kind of horrendous estimates of performance. I think I've seen this in the case of maybe hardware systems where they'll compare something like throughput, and on the graph one of the bars just looks 20 times bigger than the other, but then you actually look at the scale they're looking at and it's like, okay, they cut off the whole bottom of the graph and it's in increments of 0.1% or something. On an absolute scale this is actually not that big of a difference, but they've just really fudged the graph to make you think this is way better. Yes, that's a famous way that things can go wrong, and there's a ton of things like that.

items.question: How do you think changes in reading habits and input devices have affected the usefulness of conversation visualizations?
items.object: The influence of reading habits and input devices on conversation visualization
items.answer: One of the things that has happened is that people themselves have changed their behavior and people are much better at skimming now for two reasons. One is that I think just the way that we read online has changed a lot. People were skimming already a couple decades ago, but at this point it's just become a habit for us. The other thing is that the physical act of scrolling is far, far easier now, because it used to be a really painful thing that involved either clicking a lot of keys or actually acquiring a target with a mouse and pressing down and moving a little bit. Today it's just sort of—you’re swiping. I think it's an interesting example of how the input devices maybe affect some of the output we see. Another factor is that everyone's on their phones, and the kind of interface in that conversational thumbnails paper, where you see this very crisp, clear visualization of the entire conversation and are using that to navigate, works beautifully on a large monitor. It does not work so well on a phone. That's one of the other things that we're contending with with visualizations: how do we make them work on a small screen?

items.question: How do you think path dependence will shape the way people use machine learning?
items.object: Path dependence in how people use machine learning
items.answer: I think that there is exactly that kind of path dependence. I think as we talk about machine learning, it's really important to keep that in mind. The two lessons here are, one, that people's behaviors will change just as the technology changes, and we shouldn't assume that the way people use something like chatbots today is going to be anything like what it is in 10 years. That change may not be something that's under my control. It may be that a set of forward-looking teenagers, like so many other things in culture, end up setting the way everyone else interacts with it. That's one thing. But to your point, there's this interesting possibility that one way we might affect how people use machine learning, if we want to affect it, is to come up with an interface that has affordances for the kinds of behavior we hope people will do and maybe makes it harder to do behavior that would not be so good.

items.question: What did you learn about the value of people analyzing data together from the baby name visualization you created with your wife?
items.object: Collective data analysis through the baby name visualization
items.answer: The interesting thing that we noticed is that I think both of us had assumed that people who are interested in names were likely to be expectant parents, and what we would see is that people trying to name their kids would use this. We did see that, but something else happened that was really surprising: all of these other people around the internet started using it. They would write about it on blogs, they would write about it in discussion groups. Sometimes they'd be very explicit, like, 'I do not like children,' and they're still interested in this. So they were not expectant parents, and they would start finding things in the data. It was this surprising and cool situation where the set of data that this thing was showing was basically many thousands of names, and there were time series over the past century, roughly, of their popularity. There are a lot of patterns in there, many of them quite subtle, a lot of them coming to bear on how our culture is changing, and people collectively found a lot of these patterns. They would go back and forth and give each other little challenges. This ties into this idea that I mentioned before around there being an interesting difference between groups of people using computers versus just one person, because there was a collective dynamic around data analysis where people were collectively finding much more, I think, than any individual person would have found. This became an inspiration for me: what can we do with the collective power of people analyzing data together? I also will credit my collaborator Fernanda Viégas with having a lot of these ideas very early, and possibly earlier, where she was looking at visualizations and seeing very similar things: they were sparking conversations, and those conversations and the storytelling around them turned out to be a major part of the experience around the visualization, a major part of the value that they brought.

items.question: Why did you find Wikipedia's editing dynamics worth investigating in the History Flow project?
items.object: Wikipedia as a subject for the History Flow project
items.answer: We were drawn to Wikipedia for a couple of reasons. One is that we were both interested in looking at social activity on the web. This was already something we were both interested in. Of the people who knew about it, there were probably a few people I knew who were excited, but the majority of people I met really hated it. They thought that this was just a terrible idea, to let anyone edit an encyclopedia. Their viewpoint was, you're just going to end up with something that looks like the walls at a gas station bathroom. It's just going to be full of all sorts of crud, and you just don't want that. items.question: What did studying Wikipedia teach you about how an open editing community can govern itself?
items.object: Wikipedia’s community governance and self-healing structure
items.answer: All of the skeptics I talked to, in a certain sense, they were all right. Every single point they made about what could go wrong on Wikipedia was going wrong. You could definitely find cases for lots of pages where it did look like the walls of a gas station bathroom, where people were posting obscene things, filthy things, useless things, offensive things. They were right; all this bad stuff was happening. But what was so dramatic was that we did an analysis, and you could also see this in the visualizations: bad things got fixed by the community. They had come up with a kind of self-healing structure in which people would sign up to watch certain pages, they would get automatically alerted if things happened on those pages, and the community itself was doing a good job with the technical tools they had to moderate a lot of the bad things that would happen. Another thing that became clear as we continued to do research is that it wasn't just a few technical tools that allowed this, or people's whims and energy, but there were a lot of guidelines. Wikipedia, in some ways, after a couple of years had become noticeably bureaucratic. There were lots of policies, and when people would argue about it they would be sitting there citing chapter and verse from different pages. That was interesting too, because that was almost the opposite of what you expect of a freewheeling place that everyone could edit. The last thing you expect is a bunch of bureaucracy, and yet there it was, and it actually seemed to be pretty effective. I think a lot that I learned from this is the value of transparency tools that give you transparency, the ability of communities to take things that seem dangerous and use them in ways that actually turn out to be okay, and the value of a certain amount of process and bureaucracy. At times that really can work, as boring as it might seem.

items.question: How do you understand the usefulness of Wikipedia’s neutral point of view as an organizing principle despite its imperfections?

items.question: How do you approach the idea of understanding machine learning models?

items.question: What did you want PAIR, People + AI Research, to focus on in its approach to machine learning?
items.object: PAIR's people-centered approach to machine learning research
items.answer: This is a group that Fernanda and I started, basically to look at, okay, there's more to machine learning than just beating benchmarks and getting to state of the art on some task. Instead, what you really want to do is think about how machine learning fits into human activity in general. How can we center on people and think about how people are going to use this, how people can be part of this broader system? I don't think we were the only people thinking about this, but I think we were fairly early to create a group based on this idea. One thing that becomes clear, and this will—if you try to unpack the word understanding, you see the same thing—is that there are many different groups of people who want to do different things with a machine learning system. You might have engineers trying to figure out how to make their system perform better. You might have a doctor working with a machine learning system and wanting to use it effectively but not get drawn into illusions or misunderstand it. You might have someone using a consumer application making predictions for them of some sort. What is the right way for them to interact? Can we create guidelines for a designer of a consumer system? All of those are really different use cases, but they're all really important. We decided to tackle all of these at PAIR in different ways.

items.question: How do you think we should approach uncertainty about the future of AI and its effects on people?

items.question: What do you find especially beautiful about TensorFlow.js?

items.question: How do you interpret what visualization revealed about shared representations in Google's multilingual machine translation system?
items.object: Shared representations in Google's multilingual machine translation system
items.answer: That was a case where I think visualization was really helpful in uncovering and telling the story about a really interesting fact. The idea behind this paper—and again, I have to say there are a lot of authors who do many things on this; I was just one of a team of people here—was that you could train a system on language pairs, like you might train it to translate from Japanese into English or from Chinese into Spanish. I forget the exact pairs that were used, but if you trained on enough multilingual pairs, you could end up translating between pairs of languages where it had not seen any actual training data. That was already a very interesting result, but of course the question is: how is it doing that? One idea is that there was a shared representation, something along the lines of what linguists have called an interlingua, a kind of universal single language that you're going into. The funny thing is that there's a 1949 memorandum by Warren Weaver on translation, one of the foundational documents of AI, and he suggests this as a translation mechanism. He's like, well, maybe we're living in a building and there are all these different rooms in it, but there's a basement, and they're all connected to that. Instead of coming up with all these paths between the rooms, the right thing is just to everyone goes down to the basement and meets there, and that's how we have this one universal language. Humans have never figured out that universal language. However, it did seem like there was some sort of shared representation. If you took a sentence in English or Korean or Portuguese and mapped it and looked at the internal activation space, you would see that sentences that meant the same thing would get mapped into the same region even if they were in different languages. There was actually this shared representation. It's sort of grandiose and probably incorrect to call it a universal language, but there was something in common that it was getting at. Another interesting thing we saw in the paper, and visualization made this clear as well as analysis, was there were cases where it did not develop a shared representation, and that actually corresponded to situations where it turned out not to be able to do this kind of translation nearly as well. It was kind of cool that you could look at something geometric you saw in a visualization and actually make a prediction about performance based on that.

items.question: Why do you see calibrating users’ trust as a major design challenge for machine learning systems?
items.object: Calibrating users’ trust in machine learning systems
items.answer: One of the things that we said in a later work, the People + AI guidebook that PAIR put out, is it's not like your goal as a designer is to increase trust in your system. items.question: Why do you find both the person metaphor and the tool metaphor troublesome for understanding how to write code with a large language model like ChatGPT?
items.object: Person and tool metaphors for large language models
items.answer: One of my favorite examples that shows the complexity of design, and why this is a whole new world, is writing code with a large language model, something like ChatGPT, which I think a lot of the listeners are probably most familiar with. One point of view some people have is they think of these models as people, and there are a lot of reasons why that is actually a troublesome thing to do. One is that you might just trust it too much. You might get code and just assume everything is going to be fine, and that's not true because these things do make mistakes. There's another point of view, which is these things are just like tools, like every other tool we use, and that also is hard. There's a really interesting failure mode I've seen many times where someone is writing code with ChatGPT, they run it and discover a mistake, and they're like, well, it just didn't work. If you try to use a hammer and the hammer breaks in two, you're like, oh, that's a bad hammer, okay, I'm not going to use that. In fact, if you have experience using these systems, what you learn to do is talk back to the system and say, 'I ran that code and got the following error, got the following undesirable thing. Can you fix it?' Very often it will fix it, and that, in my experience, makes it many times more powerful than if you just expect a right answer the first time. What's interesting to me is that the first two metaphors that as a designer you'd reach for—a metaphor of a person or a metaphor of a tool—both get you in trouble. One of the exciting points of design right now, and probably for a while to come, is to figure out: do we use metaphor at all? Do we come up with new vocabulary for this? How do we teach people how to use these things? I think it's a fascinating area.

items.question: How do you approach the question of whether language models build internal models of the world?
items.object: Internal world models in language models and the Othello experiment
items.answer:
One of the things that I've been fascinated by at an intellectual level is: with large language models, to what degree can we think of them as aggregating statistics? A word one hears is the famous paper that refers to them as stochastic parrots and describes these as a haphazard collection of statistics, versus are they doing something like trying to build an internal model of the world that they are encountering? It's really unclear. I don't know what they're doing; it's hard to say even now, I think, but it's a really interesting scientific question. One of the ways I try to operationalize it is saying, okay, are there internal models that we could probe? Could we look at the activations as the LLM is chugging along during inference and make a guess ourselves as to what it thinks about the world? I'll put the word 'think' in quotes; I probably shouldn't even use it here. What aspects of the world is it encoding in order to make a prediction?

One piece of research that came from my lab, led by Kenneth Lee, is that we took a game, a simple game called Othello, that many people played in school. We did a little experiment: we said all right, we'll train a language model. It doesn't really know anything about language, so we're thinking of it basically as a sequence model, on just transcripts of Othello games, both generated by people and ones generated by a computer playing against itself. Then we're going to see, number one, does it learn to make legal moves? In other words, if you give it the beginning of a game, will it predict the next move in a way that actually would fit the rules? The answer is it does, which is weird because what we train on are just transcripts. It doesn't know there's a game, it doesn't know there's a board; it just sees the squares where things get played.

There's a whole other set of work where people have refined exactly what this model looks like and discovered it's even simpler than what we found in our paper, but it really feels like when you actually probe for this thing, not only does it make legal moves, but it's using a representation of the board to make those moves. It's a complicated story, not a simple situation, but roughly speaking there appears to be a model in there. Whether a giant language model has the same set of internals, I don't know, but we could start to ask: what if it does? What if there are interpretable aspects of the internals of these models, and could we use those to our advantage?

items.question: Why do you think a chatbot's internal representation of its user is worth making visible?
items.object: A chatbot's internal representation of its user
items.answer:
My collaborator Fernanda grew up in Brazil and she often will talk to ChatGPT in Portuguese. In Portuguese, morphologically, the language is such that you sometimes just have to make a decision whether you're talking to someone who's male or female, just the way certain words work. What she noticed is that typically ChatGPT would start out addressing her as male, but there could be certain triggers—for example, if she mentioned something about wearing a dress to a formal lunch—that would make it switch, and then from then on it would address her as female. That's an interesting phenomenon. It's not wildly surprising given that it is a good language model; you'd expect an effective language model might do things like that. But now we can ask how it's doing that. If the answer is that there is some internal representation of the user where gender has just changed, that becomes interesting. You might think to yourself, you know, it's cool that Fernanda can see that talking to it in Portuguese, but what about English? We might want to know.

This ties into other work where some of these models will tell you what you want to hear, this idea of sycophancy, where they kind of guess your political beliefs and if you ask a political question they'll give an answer tailored to you. For all of these reasons you might think, okay, probably it's important to know what the system is thinking of me at any given time, partly so I can interpret, so I can calibrate trust in the answers. If you're concerned about safety, if you're concerned about the machine doing something that could have negative consequences and it's not obvious from the words I'm seeing on screen, maybe there's some way you could probe and get a sense of, oh, it's in this zone that is potentially going to be dangerous. For all sorts of reasons, getting a sense of how you are represented in the network is very interesting.

items.question: How do you see a chatbot's representation of itself becoming useful in dashboard design?
items.object: The system model and chatbot dashboards in 'The System Model and the User Model'
items.answer:
There's a second representation that feels like it's probably primal: how does the system represent itself? One thing I notice is these systems are good both at producing content that looks like nonfiction or producing content that looks like fiction. When it's producing content that looks like fiction, it will talk about magic and do all sorts of stuff that has nothing to do with what would actually happen in the real world, whereas when it's producing nonfiction, it feels like it will do things like that less. We know you can't really trust everything it says, and there are certainly hallucinations, but it's almost like a different mode. You might ask yourself, is there a real difference here, and would it be useful to know if I think it is producing something like nonfiction—I'm asking it to summarize a certain Python API, for example—and I suddenly see it's gone into fiction mode? That might be a sign that I need to pay close attention. This is what we call the system model.

This paper is speculative and conjectural, but the premise is we can find models inside these models, the equivalent of a mental model, whatever that might mean for a large language model. There are a couple of these things that are especially important: how the user is represented and how the system is represented. Then we say, okay, let's think about how we might make dashboards, because all of the complicated systems we use in our life, and even not complicated ones like coffee makers, are full of little blinking lights that tell us about their internal state. Why shouldn't chatbots be the same?

items.question: How do you assess the causal evidence that Othello-GPT uses an internal model of the board?
items.object: Causal evidence for an internal board model in Othello-GPT
items.answer: One thing I will say is that we did do some causal experiments in there. In particular, what we were able to do is take positions, run them partway through the network under inference, then make a change that our previous work would predict would change the internal model—so a square would change from white to black—and that would change its prediction in the end in a way that was consonant with what we had done. We made those changes even on positions that would be impossible to reach through any kind of game, so we knew for 100% sure they were not in its training dataset. There I would say there was a causal link. I will say that there's been follow-up work with Neil and Andrew Lee that just came out, where we're looking at even simpler representations Neil found. It is a complicated story where what you can see is that for much of the game it seems like these representations are really important. It does look like maybe in the end game it is doing something a little bit different.

items.question: What kind of skepticism do you find most productive when studying how neural networks memorize and generalize?
items.object: Scientific skepticism about memorization and generalization in neural networks
items.answer: One of the things I think is very deceptive scientifically in all of these things, and why it's so difficult, is that the phenomenon that I think is pretty well established at this point is that when you have a neural network it's usually doing some combination of memorization and generalization. If you are looking for things that are perfect generalization, you'll never find anything that's 100% there, but you can often find some. If you're looking for an example of where it memorizes something, you can usually find that too. You can usually find some evidence of generalization. It's very, very complicated, and so I think understanding the nuances is really important. That level of skepticism is really good. The most productive kind of skepticism is to be in the mode of, 'What's going on? Is that really what's happening?' rather than, 'Is that particular thing true?' or 'Does this fit my preconceived notions?' Sometimes people are skeptical in a way that favors their prior beliefs, and that's a thing to watch out for.

items.question: Why do you see even partial transparency into a system as a useful guideline for interface design?
items.object: Partial transparency into computer and human systems
items.answer: One direction is giving users transparency into what's going on. If you have some level, even partial, of transparency into a system, that historically has just been incredibly useful in all sorts of computer systems—in fact, every system. It's true of human systems too. Why do people look at stock market indices? That was a big invention, the idea of averaging all the stocks that were available, or some important subset. Before that people didn't quite realize; they had no way of seeing what was going on in the market. In general even partial kinds of transparency have historically been really helpful. That would be the first guideline.

items.question: Why did you find Hewitt and Manning's work on syntax-tree geometry in BERT so inspiring?
items.object: Hewitt and Manning's work on syntax-tree geometry in BERT
items.answer: There's work from Hewitt and Manning that I read, a paper that I don't know how to describe except to say it kind of just exploded in my brain. I loved this paper so much. They were looking at BERT, basically a Transformer model, in which—I'm going to dramatically oversimplify because we don't have a whiteboard here, but the model that should be in your head is we have a series of word embeddings for each word of a sentence. I'm oversimplifying key details around tokens and all sorts of things, but bear with me here. The model sits there and at each step modifies those embeddings a little bit, and eventually it gets to a point where, if you look at each of those embeddings as a point in a high-dimensional space, there is a sort of linear transformation you can do, and remarkably those points form a tree in space that is the same as the syntax tree, the kind of syntax tree you get if you diagram the sentence. items.question: How did you make sense of the squared Euclidean distance relationship in Hewitt and Manning's syntax-tree embeddings?
items.object: The squared Euclidean distance relationship in BERT's syntax-tree embeddings
items.answer: There's a funny mathematical thing: their version of the tree, the way they found it, was to say, look, if you look at the distance between any two words, the tree distance in the syntax tree, and take the square of the Euclidean distance between the corresponding embedding points, that will correspond. I remember wondering, why would it be the square? Why not the actual distance? If you sit down and fiddle around with pencil and paper for a while, you can realize that it's basically impossible for arbitrary trees to use Euclidean distance and tree distance and have it be consonant; you can actually work out what essentially the unique solution is that allows the distance to be a Euclidean distance. It's this very beautiful kind of embedding where everything is at right angles, which works in high-dimensional space. If you go back and look, and we have references in the paper, there are math papers from the '30s that talk about some of these ideas. They were often ahead of the curve. Basically, we were able to say here's the shape that these things take. There's been other follow-up work from Chris Manning's group that goes into more detail on this and tells you what some of the directions might be that correspond to syntax in particular ways.

items.question: What made your work on mapping word meanings from BERT embeddings especially compelling to you?
items.object: Word-sense geometry and the online atlas of word meanings
items.answer: Then there's a part where we said, well, syntax is one thing; what about semantics, the meanings of these words? We said let's do something completely opposite: look at word senses. A classic question in natural language processing is when someone uses a word like 'bank,' do they mean a financial bank, a river bank? Word senses are very, very subtle. It turns out to be a very difficult task to figure out which dictionary sense of a word someone is using. What we discovered is that if you find a transformation, again a different one than the one used for syntax, that makes sense, it will let you highlight the semantic meaning of the word that is being chosen in a way that you can actually build classifiers that at that point got state of the art against some standard classifiers for identifying word senses. To tie in visualization, we created an atlas online that I think is called the Atlas of Meaning. Emily led this, and it should be up today. It lets you type in a word and see a map of the different contexts in which it's used. Maybe it's called the Context Atlas; I'll follow up with that. It lets you see a map of meanings that in many ways is much more nuanced than what you would see in a dictionary. One thing that really stuck out to me is how it will separate metaphorical and literal meanings of words. If you type in the word 'lens,' you get a map where you’re very far away from the lens of a telescope to 'let's look at this in a sociological lens,' and it's very cool to see all these things pop out and say, okay, I'm actually getting a visualization of language. items.question: Why do you find next-word prediction an inadequate way to explain large language models to people?
items.object: Explaining large language models as next-word predictors
items.answer: People will often try to explain large language models by focusing on the next-word-prediction aspect. People have this good motivation that they want to provide intuition for what's happening. However, I too am always surprised by what they're doing. Thinking of these systems as next-word predictors is really not a great way of building your intuition, because their behavior doesn't fit with that at all. For me, the moment where this hit was GPT-3, where someone had the example of asking the system to just translate smoothly between English and French using a prompt. I never would have guessed that just next-word prediction would lead to that. I don't know the best way we're going to explain these systems to people, but I feel like next-word prediction is a slightly deceptive way to describe it at this point. It's technically true, although once you add training with instruction tuning or RLHF and stuff it becomes less true. There's certainly truth to it, but I don't think it's a great way of building intuition.

items.question: What do you find revealing about visualizing music by connecting repeated sections with arcs?
items.object: Visualizing musical repetition with arcs
items.answer: A constant question in my career is trying to figure out what do things look like, to observe things in new ways. I gave myself this challenge at one point: I want to make pictures of music. Not the first person to think about this, but it's a fun question. One thing that you can do if you look at a music score is observe that there's a lot of repetition there. It's not a novel observation, but there it is. The thing I realized is that if you visualize the repetition itself—if you took a timeline of a piece of music and looked at one section and just connected it with an arc to the next section where that repeats—if it repeats, you start to see this almost fractal kind of beauty in the music that is out there. I think this reflects the deep complexity of the music; it certainly does not capture the full complexity at all. When I've talked to musicians about the visualizations you get from this, there often is a little bit of ambivalence. People say, 'But I can't hear anything. You're not really getting it across.' At the same time there's a surprise about the complexity, about just the patterns you get. It becomes one more exercise in translation, I guess. Not to force too much of a metaphor here, it's a nice example of how looking at something very simple about the music—in this case just repetition—if you do that at scale, more than any human would have the patience to do, but a computer can sit and look for every possible repetition in a long piece of music, it can create something that gives you a larger whole where it has these emergent properties that come out. For me this was a very satisfying set of artworks to do because I would sit there and spend time with a machine I could feed a piece of music into, and suddenly see this internal structure come out. Some of them were especially beautiful. I was like, oh, Philip Glass, everything he does actually looks really, really good. There are others where a lot of jazz is interesting: at the beginning you'll see these very regular structures and then it will hit the point where it goes beyond what I think the computer can really process, and I think that's beautiful too as a metaphor.

items.question: What do you find intellectually exciting about the surprising capabilities of AI systems trained with simple techniques such as next-word prediction?
items.object: The surprising capabilities of AI systems trained with simple techniques such as next-word prediction
items.answer: It ties back to this idea of things happening at multiple scales. I think that is one of the big intellectual mysteries we're all trying to unravel: to what degree do these systems reproduce these multiple scales? When do they not? What is really disorienting about this whole field is that we have these systems that we built, use things like very simple techniques like next-word prediction to train them, and then they end up doing stuff that is really surprising. They do it through this mysterious combination: some stuff seems to be memorization, some stuff seems to be going beyond that. We don't quite know what that is. To me it's really, really exciting. I think this is just one of the most intellectually interesting things to happen in my lifetime.

items.question: How do you hope collective curiosity will help people make sense of unfamiliar AI technology?
items.object: Curiosity as a way to understand unfamiliar AI technology
items.answer: I think what I hope to see is people gathering more information. When I described a title of a hypothetical book as I Don't Know, and Neither Does Anyone Else, it's not meant to be nihilistic at all. Instead, it's about curiosity, I think, and what I'm hoping for is that our collective curiosity can get us through this. Some of the technology we have is just really strange, and we all use metaphors to try to make sense of it, but at the end of the day it's its own thing, and the more that we can explore it the better.

items.question: How would you like experimentation with AI interfaces to develop over the next three years?
items.object: Experimentation with AI interfaces
items.answer: What I hope in terms of what I would like to see in the next three years for interfaces is lots of interfaces. I remember in the early days of the worldwide web—I was there for that, and that was my job—it was really exciting to see the early websites, and every website looked a little bit different. Sometimes the navigation was on the left, sometimes on the right, sometimes there was no navigation. People tried all sorts of things, and that was really important. In the end, today most websites kind of look the same. It's a little tedious, but at the same time we've realized what works and what doesn't, which is very nice. I would think about this moment as like the early days of the web, and I think we need a lot of exploration. I'm hoping that we try different things and see what happens. We don't necessarily prejudge what's going to work and what isn't. There are certain cases that are very high stakes where all sorts of things could go wrong, where we do need to be very careful and think way in advance. But I'm hoping there are enough lower-stakes cases where we can really experiment and see what works and what doesn't.

items.question: How would you like the balance between observation and theory in AI research to change?
items.object: Observation and theory in AI research
items.answer: The most important thing I want to see is more observations. I think theorizing is interesting; I theorize for a living, I love to theorize, and I want more theory too. But as a field there is way too much emphasis on coming up with a theory, coming up with a normative version of what the world should do, and not enough stopping and looking around and saying what is actually happening. I would like to see experiments to try a lot of things out, and academic conferences being very friendly to pure observational papers that just say, look, we studied this thing and we saw this, we saw X, we don't know why it happens, but we didn't see this, and it was really important, and maybe someone else can figure it out.
